title.narrative: Durable Solutions Through Community Resilience - IOM/FAO/UN Habitat
Hållbara Lösningar genom ökad resiliens hos lokalsamhällen - IOM/FAO/UN Habitat

description.narrative:
The overarching objective is to "contribute to durable solutions through improved conditions for sustainable socio-economic recovery and peaceful co-existence of disaster-affected communities with particular attention to the most vulnerable groups while strengthening local government capacity in responding to the needs of internal displacement".
To promote the provision of sustainable support allowing for short to medium to long-term development, project operations are two-staged where activities take place both in locations of displacement identifying and supporting households with return, relocation, and (re)integration, while simultaneously intervening in hosting communities to support socio-economic (re)integration through a whole of society area-based interventions.
The programme has 4 specific outcomes, each UN partner responsible for one outcome each, with the fourth outcome being joint for ensuring complementarity, coordination, lessons learnt, etc.:
Outcome 1: Target communities are supported to relocate, return, and (re)integrate through the implementation of community-based planning and multi-sectoral recovery interventions aimed at building community cohesion and resilience (main responsible IOM)
Outcome 2: Enhanced economic status of the vulnerable members in the displacement-affected communities through facilitated opportunities for livelihood diversification options through on-farm and off-farm interventions and increased access to finance (main responsible FAO)
Outcome 3: Regional and woreda administrations can facilitate sustainable reintegration of IDPs through the woreda development (main responsible UN Habitat)
Outcome 4: The Governments capacity in mainstreaming durable solutions in its programmes is maintained and enhanced (All UN agencies)
The project targets 56,396 displacement-affected persons, including host-communities over 4 years and is implemented in the Somali and Oromia regional states of Ethiopia that experienced massive displacement in 2026 and 2017 along their respective borders due to inter-ethnic/-communal tensions and disputes, mainly related to land and water resources. The partners have included IDP camps, sites and settlements, as well locations where IDPs are relocated or returning to, altogether 8 sites:
Oromia regional state: Miesso woreda, Gende Buno; Babile woreda, Darer Arba, Qoloji; Chinakson woreda, Gella.
Somali regional state: Erer woreda, Magalo-ad; Awbare woreda, Awbare Relocation site; Kebribayah woreda, Dhurwale; Godey woreda, Bayahew.

Programmet "Strengthening Resilience of Disaster Affected Communities through Durable Solutions in Oromia and Somali Regions of Ethiopia" ligger inom ramen för Durable Solutions Framework, och genomförs i samarbete mellan tre FN-organ: Förenta Nationernas (FN) Internationella Organisation för Migration (IOM), FNs Livsmedels- och jordbruksorganisation (FAO) samt FNs Program för Mänsklig Bosättning (UN Habitat).
Det övergripande målet är att bidra till hållbara lösningar genom förbättrade villkor för hållbar socioekonomisk återhämtning och fredlig samexistens mellan internflyktingar och värdsamhällen, med särskild uppmärksamhet på de mest utsatta, i kombination med stöd till lokala myndigheter för att stärka deras kapacitet att möta internflyktingars behov. Med vägledning av ett samhällscentrerat operativt ramverk syftar projektet till att uppnå föreslagna mål i enlighet med DSI-strategins nyckelområden, med insatser på operativ, planerings-, policy-, lagstiftnings- och institutionell nivå. Kopplingen mellan de tre specialiserade FN-organen kommer, genom samordnade integrerade tillvägagångssätt som syftar till att skapa rättsligt, materiellt och fysiskt skydd för fördrivna samhällen, skapa synergier mellan operativa aktiviteter för kopplingar mellan stad och landsbygd, fredlig samexistens, försörjning, tillgång till bostäder, mark , och egendom (HLP), och tillgång till grundläggande tjänster.

The programme "Strengthening Resilience of Disaster Affected Communities through Durable Solutions in Oromia and Somali Regions of Ethiopia" is under the Durable Solutions Framework, and will be implemented through the collaborative efforts of three UN agencies: International Organisation for Migration (IOM), United Nations Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), and the United Nations Human Settlement Program (UN Habitat). IOM will be the contracting partner, and the lead agency for the programme.
The overarching objective is to contribute to durable solutions through improved conditions for sustainable socio-economic recovery and peaceful co-existence of disaster-affected communities with particular attention to most vulnerable groups while strengthening local government capacity in responding to the needs of internal displacement. Guided by a community-centered operational framework, the project aims to achieve proposed objectives framed around the key pillars of the DSI strategy, with interventions at operational, planning, policy, legislative, and institutional levels. The linkage between the three specialised UN agencies will, through coordinated integrated approaches aimed at generating legal, material, and physically protection for displacement affected communities, create synergies between operational activities for urban-rural linkages, community cohesion, livelihood, access to housing, land, and property (HLP), and access to basic services.

sector.narrative: Facilitation of orderly, safe, regular and responsible migration and mobility

description.narrative:
In 2025, the project made significant progress in implementation of efforts to advance durable solutions for displacement-affected communities across Oromia and Somali Regions. Some examples of results achieved during the year are summarized as follows.
Safe Relocation and Community Reintegration
The relocation of 532 IPD HHs from Qoloji camp to Bayahaw was completed in year 2024. The effort to establishing their livelihoods and other durable solutions initiatives has continued through 2025. A total of 806 HHs, 532 HHs relocated and 274 HHs vulnerable host community received cash assistance to meet immediate needs, strengthen coping capacity and support recovery following relocation. To imporove access to basic services and reinforce intergaration efforts, several community-driven priority infrastructures, comprising schools and animal feed centres, were constructed across target woredas. For relocation and reintegration efforts to remain safe, inclusive, and responsive, 21 community consultations and perception assessments were conducted, with special attention to vulnerable groups.
Community-based planning processes were strengthened through the development of a Community Action Plan (CAP) for Bayahaw, establishment of a Community Management Committee, and engagement of government authorities and partners through a multi-stakeholder roundtable that strengthened coordination and joint planning efforts.
In terms of strengthening social cohesion, newly established and strengthened peace committees enhanced conflict resolution capacities, while 16 community dialogues, six conflict analysis consultations, a large-scale peace conference, and seven inter-woreda coordination mechanisms promoted peaceful coexistence and cooperation between communities in Oromia and Somali regions. In addition, four sports-for-peace events engaged over 1,200 participants, contributing to improved social cohesion. Community priorities were addressed through the construction and rehabilitation of four community infrastructures, including schools and animal feed centers.
Among conflict-affected respondents, 79 percent recognized the existence of community conflict prevention and resolution mechanisms, although 21 percent viewed, highlighting limited accessibility and delays in dispute resolution. Overall satisfaction with project assistance was very high at 95 percent, with female respondents reporting slightly higher satisfaction levels than males.
Livelihoods, Economic Recovery and Climate Resilience
Under the quitable and better access to economic opportunities initiative, the project condiderably improved livelihood opportunities and resilience.
A total of 887 hectares of rangeland and 728 hectares of dryland were rehabilitated across the five project districts, enhancing sustainable land management and environmental restoration. More than 540 government experts and 912 farmer received training in climate-smart agriculture, natural resource management, and improved agronomic practices. Agricultural inputs were distributed to 870 households, enabling cultivation across 517 hectares. The verage annual household income increased significantly from ETB 22,590 at baseline to ETB 62,867. The development of small scale solar pump irrigation scheme is underway completing feasibility study and design of the schedme. Economic recovery was further supported through cash-based interventions, including USD 384,000 in cash-for-work payments and USD 53,400 in unconditional cash transfers for newly relocated households. Households use the cash to meet their basic needs as well as some for livelihood investment. Livelihood diversification support reached 1,262 households that did not participate in Cash for Work, providing livestock and production inputs, and livelihood diversification training that strengthened food security and income generation. 54 percent of respondents of a recent joint monitoring survey reported that they have adopted at least one new farming or production practice, 13 percent adopting several and 33% have not made any changes, suggestung persistent gaps in access to information and support systems.
The project also promoted off-farm livelihoods through grants and business support to improve household income and access to market.
Three community-managed Animal Feed Centers were established in Oromia and received USD 24,000 in start-up capital. They have started to earn an average monthly profit of ETB 15,000 per center, members initiated individual livelihood activities using dividends. Ten Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), including seven women-owned businesses, received the first disbursement of USD 21,000 after signing binding milestone agreements, while 14 women-led Village Economic and Social Groups benefitting 137 women received training and start-up grants totaling USD 17,500. Additionally, 165 households completed entrepreneurship training and received USD 49,500 in business start-up capital. Approximately, USD 15,000 was distributed to 146 HHs participated in CfW activitis in Bayahaw relocation site. Local sustainability was enhanced through a Training of Trainers programme for 14 business coaches and engagement of government stakeholders.
Strengthening Institutional Capacity and Risk Management
Government capacity was strengthened through settlement-planning training reaching 211 government officials and technical experts. Among the trainees, 41 technical experts were trained in Housing, Land and Property (HLP), Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Remote Sensing to improve disaster preparedness and risk-informed planning. Trained personnel have actively contributed to settlement planning processes, preparation of occupancy certificates, and use of GIS and remote sensing tools to inform evidence-based decision-making.
Updated disaster risk profiles were developed for seven woredas, an analytical report was produced examining displacement drivers and impacts in Oromia and Somali regions, while hydrological studies and corresponding flood and drought response plans provided evidence-based guidance for future risk mitigation. Environmental resilience was further enhanced through a tree-planting initiative involving 208 community members and the planting of 1,000 trees in Dhurwale relocation site.
Important progress was achieved in settlement planning and access to housing. Settlement plans for six project sites were finalized in addition to the two that were finalized in 2024, once endorsed by the government offices it will create the foundation for improved access to land information and sustainable settlements. Housing repair kits were distributed to 200 households, and 80 community members received practical construction skills training. Infrastructure development included the completion of two mud-block production sheds for youth cooperatives promoting owner-driven durable and affordable housing. Based on vulnerability criteria, 108 housing units are being upgraded in Meiso town and the construction of 40 durable housing units using innovative jute fiber reinforced concrete technology has been launched in Magalacad relocation site. Construction of houses for newly identified and registered 376 IDP HHs is ongoing in Goriyawol and anticipated to be completed before relocation. The project also improved environmental sanitation through waste management infrastructures like dumping pits and awareness activities.
Furthermore, housing, land and property (HLP) rights were promoted through title deed and occupancy certificate issuance, stakeholder consultations, and capacity-building initiatives.
Enhanced Durable Solutions Coordination
At regional, zonal, and national levels, the project reinforced durable solutions coordination mechanisms. Durable Solutions Working Groups remained active in Somali, Oromia, and Tigray regions, while the national, UN-led, Solutions Working Group expanded its membership and strengthened federal-regional coordination. The project also supported the mapping of durable solutions interventions nationwide and the DSWG facilitated dialogue on the transformation of Qoloji IDP camp into a permanent settlement, advancing local integration and sustainable solutions for displaced populations.
